question: Four charges, each charge $q$ coloumb are placed at points $(-1,0,0),(1,0,0),(0,-1,0)$ and $(0,1,0)$ in the $x y$ - plane. The distances along the axes are measured in meters. The magnitude of the electric field at the point $z=1 m$ on the $z-$ axis is

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: The given situation is shown below. According to given situation we have to find electric field at point $P(0,0,1)$ . Distance of point $P$ from each charges is equal to $\sqrt{1^2+1^2}=\sqrt{2}$ $E_{A P}\;=E_{B P}=E_{C P}=E_{D P}=\;\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \cdot \;\frac{q}{(\sqrt{2})^2}$ $\;=\;\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \cdot \;\frac{q}{2}$ $E_{A P}$ and $E_{B P}$ are perpendicular to each other. Let $E'$ be the resultant electric field of $E_{A P}$ and $E_{B P}$ , then $E'\;=\sqrt{E_{A P}^2+E_{B P}^2}=\sqrt{2 E_{A P}^2} . \; \; [\because E_{A P}=E_{B P}]$ $\;=E_{A P} \sqrt{2}$ $\;=\;\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \;\frac{q\sqrt{2}}{2}=\;\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \;\frac{q}{\sqrt{2}}$ $E'\;=\;\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \;\frac{q}{\sqrt{2}}$ In the similar way, net electric field due to $E_{C P}$ and $E_{p p}$ $E''=\;\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \cdot \;\frac{q}{\sqrt{2}}$ Again $E'$ and $E''$ are directed in same direction i.e along $+z$ direction, hence net electric field, $E_{\;\text{net }\;}=E'+E''=2 E'$ $[\because E'=E'']$ $=2\;\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\;\frac{q}{\sqrt{2}}=\;\frac{q}{2\sqrt{2} \pi \varepsilon_0} \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{C}$ © examsnet.com

question: A capacitor of capacitance $C_{1}=10\;\mu\text{F}$ to charged using $9\;\text{V}$ battery. It is then removed from the battery and connected to another capacitor $C_{2}=20\;\mu\text{F}$ as shown in the figure. The charge on $C_{2}$ after equilibrium has reached is

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given, $C_{1}\;=10\;\mu\text{F}$ $\;=10^{-5}\;\text{F}$ $V_{1}\;=9\;\text{V}$ Charge on capacitor $C_{1}$ , $q_{1}\;=C_{1}V_{1}$ $\;=9\times10^{-5}\;\text{C}$ $C_{2}\;=20\;\mu\text{F}=2\times10^{-5}\;\text{F}$ when uncharged capacitor $C_{2}$ is connected with charged capacitor $C_{1}$ , then charges will flow from capacitor $C_{1}$ to $C_{2}$ till both gain the same potential i.e common potential. Common potential, $V=\frac{\;\text{ total charge }\;}{\;\text{ total capacitance }\;}$ $\;=\frac{q_{1}}{C_{1}+C_{2}}=\frac{9\times10^{-5}}{10^{-5}+2\times10^{-5}}$ $\;=\frac{9\times10^{-5}}{3\times10^{-5}}=3\;\text{V}$ Charge on capacitor $C_{2},\;q_{2}=C_{2}V$ $=2\times10^{-5}\times3=6\times10^{-5}\;\text{C}$ © examsnet.com

question: Two parallel plate capacitors $8\,\mu\mathrm{F}$ each are connected in parallel to a $10\,\mathrm{V}$ battery. The plate separation in one of the capacitor is reduced to $40\%$ of its initial value. The increase in the total charge stored on the capacitors is

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given, $C_1\;=C_2=8\,\mu\mathrm{F}=8\times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{F}$ $V\;=10\,\mathrm{V}$ Since, $C_1$ and $C_2$ are connected in parallel. Equivalent capacitance, $C_{ev}=C_1+C_2=8\times 10^{-6}+8\times 10^{-6}=1.6\times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{F}$ Total charge, $q_i=C_{eq}\cdot V$ $\;=1.6\times 10^{-5}\times 10$ $\;=1.6\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{C}$ We know that, capacitance $C=\;\frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$ $\Rightarrow C\propto\frac{1}{d}$ $\Rightarrow\;\frac{C'}{C''}=\;\frac{d''}{d'}=\;\frac{d'-40\%\ \text{of}\ d}{d'}=\;\frac{\frac{3}{5}d'}{d'}$ $\Rightarrow\;\frac{C^r}{C''}=\;\frac{3}{5}$ $\Rightarrow C''=\;\frac{5}{3}C'$ $\;=\;\frac{5}{3}\times 8\times 10^{-6}=\;\frac{40}{3}\times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C}$ New capacitance, $C'''=C''+C_2$ $\;=\;\frac{40}{3}\times 10^{-6}+8\times 10^{-6}$ $\;=\;\frac{64}{3}\times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{F}$ Now value of total charge, $q_f=C'''\times V$ $\;=\;\frac{64}{3}\times 10^{-6}\times 10$ $\;=\;\frac{64}{3}\times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{C}$ Increased value of charge, $\Delta q\;=q_f-q_1$ $\;=\;\frac{64}{3}\times 10^{-5}-1.6\times 10^{-4}$ $\;=\;\frac{160}{3}\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ © examsnet.com

question: A particle of mass $1 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$ and charge $1 \times 10^{-16} \text{ C}$ enters the uniform magnetic field within the solenoid, at speed $1000 \text{ m} \text{ s}^{-1}$ . The velocity vector makes an angle $60^{\circ}$ with the axis of solenoid. The solenoid has 5000 turns along its length and carries current $5 \text{ A}$ . The number of revolutions the particle makes along the helical path within the solenoid by the time it emerges from solenoid's opposite end is

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: The given situation is shown below. Given, $v=1000 \text{ m/s}$ $\;q=10^{-16} \text{ C}$ $\;m=1 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$ $N=$ Number of turns $=5000$ $I=5 \text{ A}$ $R=$ Radius of circular path of charge Magnetic field, $B=\mu_0 n I$ (where, $n=$ number of turns per unit length) $\Rightarrow B=\mu_0 \; \frac{N}{L} I$ (where, $n=\;\frac{N}{L}$ ) $\; \Rightarrow B=\mu_0 \times \; \frac{5000}{L} \times 5$ $\; \Rightarrow B=\mu_0 \times \; \frac{25000}{L}$ ........(i) Also we know that, Distance $=$ speed $\times$ time $L=v_x \times t$ (where, $v_x$ is the component of velocity along the axis of the solenoid) $\Rightarrow \;\; L=500 t$ ......(ii) Also, radius of circular path of a charged particle in uniform magnetic field is given by the formula $R=\; \frac{m v_y}{9 B}$ $(.$ where, $v_y=500 \sqrt{3})$ Putting, $B=\; \frac{\mu_0 \times 25000}{L}$ [from Eq .(i)] $\Rightarrow \;\; R=\; \frac{10^{-11} \times \sqrt{3} L}{50 \mu_0}$ ......(ii) Now, time taken by the charged particle to exit the solenoid moving along the circular path making $N^{'}$ number of revolutions. $\;t^{'}=\frac{\; \text{circular distance} \;}{v_y} \Rightarrow t^{'}=\frac{2 \pi R \times \; \text{no. of revolutions} \;}{v_y}$ $\;t^{'}=\frac{2 \pi R \times N^{'}}{v_y}$ $t^{'}=\frac{2 \pi \times 10^{-11} \times \sqrt{3} L \times N^{'}}{50 \mu_0 \times 500 \sqrt{3}}$ .....(iii) Now, since time taken to cover linear distance and circular distance before exiting the solenoid are same $t=t^{'}$ So, from Eqs. (i) and (ii) $\;\frac{L}{500}=\frac{2 \pi \times 10^{-11} \times \sqrt{3} \times L \times N^{'}}{50 \times 4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \times 500 \sqrt{3}} \;\; (\because \mu_0=4 \pi \times 10^{-7})$ On solving, we get $N^{'} = \frac{100 \times 10^{-7}}{10^{-11}} = \frac{10^{-5}}{10^{-11}} = 10^6$ Hence, total number of revolution along helical path by the time it emerges the solenoid $=1 \times 10^6$ . Hence, option (b) is the correct answer. © examsnet.com

Hence, on equatorial line, the two fields add up As null points are on the axis of the bar magnet, therefore, $B_1 = \\; \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \\; \frac{2M}{d^3} = H$ on the equitorial line of magnet at same distance (d), field due to the magnet is $B_2 = \\; \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \\; \frac{M}{d^3} = \\; \frac{B_1}{2} = \\; \frac{H}{2}$ Therefore, total magnetic field at this point on equitorial line is $B = B_2 + H = \\; \frac{3H}{2} = \\; \frac{3}{2} \times H$ Since, given $B=0.69$ $0.6 = \\; \frac{3}{2} \times H \Rightarrow H = \\; \frac{0.6 \times 2}{3} = 0.4\ \text{G}$ © examsnet.com

solution: Solution: Given, $E = E_0 \sin \; [ (1.57 \times 10^{7} \text{m}^{-1}) (x - c t) ]$ ......(i) Work function, $\phi_0 = 1.9 \text{ eV} = 1.9 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$ Given, planck's constant, $h = 6.64 \times 10^{-34} \text{J-s}$ We know that, $h v = \phi_0 + e V_0$ (Photoelectric equation)......(ii) Where, $h v =$ incident energy of one photon $\phi_0 =$ work function of metal $\dot{e} =$ charge of an electron $V_0 =$ stopping potential Now, from Eq. (i) Clearly $\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} = 1.57 \times 10^7$ $\Rightarrow \; \frac{2 \times 314}{\lambda} = 1.57 \times 10^7 \Rightarrow \lambda = \frac{2 \times 314}{1.57 \times 10^7} = 4 \times 10^{-7}$ Now, from Eq. subject: Physics
question: Statement (A): As one considers orbits with higher values of $n$ in hydrogen atom, the electric potential energy of the atom increases. Statement (B): In Thomson's model, an atom is a spherical cloud of positive charges with electrons embedded in it. Statement (C): The orbital picture in Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom was consistent with the uncertainty principle.

options.A: A, B and C are true
options.B: A, B true, but C false
options.C: B, C true, but A false
options.D: A, C true but B false

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: In hydrogen atom, potential energy of electron in $n$ th orbit is given as $PE = \;\frac{-K z e^{2}}{r}$ ......(i) For higher value of $n, r$ increase because $r \propto n^{2}$ . From eq (i), it is clear that for higher value of $n$ , potential energy increases. Hence, statement (A) is correct. In thomson's model an atom is a spherical cloud of positive charges with electrons embedded in it. Hence, statement (B) is correct. According to Bohr's model an electron in an atom is located at a definite distance from the nucleus and is revolving with a definite velocity around it. According to heisenberg's uncertainty principle, it is impossible to determine the exact position and momentum of moving electron simultaneously. Therefore, Bohr's model of an atom is contradicted by heisenbergs uncertainty principle. The statement $(C)$ is incorrect. Hence, option (b) is correct. © examsnet.com

solution: Solution: Componentof force response for horizontal motion is $F \cos \theta$ So, acceleration of bar, $a = \frac{F \cos \theta}{m}$ As acceleration, $a = \frac{dv}{dt}$ , we have $\Rightarrow \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{F \cos \theta}{m}$ we can also express this as, $\Rightarrow \frac{dv}{dx} \cdot \frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{F \cos \theta}{m}$ $\Rightarrow v dv = \frac{F \cos \theta}{m} dx$ Integrating both sides and putting $\theta = kx$ , we get $\int v dv = \int \frac{F \cos kx}{m} dx$ $\Rightarrow \frac{v^2}{2} = \frac{F}{m} \int \cos kx \cdot dx$ $\Rightarrow \frac{v^2}{2} = \frac{F}{m} \cdot \left(\frac{\sin kx}{k}\right)$ $\Rightarrow v^2 = \frac{2F \sin kx}{m k}$ $\Rightarrow v = \sqrt{\frac{2F \sin \theta}{m k}}$ © examsnet.com

question: A block of mass $5\text{ kg}$ starts up a $45^{\circ}$ incline plane with initial kinetic energy of $100\text{ J}$ . If the coefficient of friction between block and plane is $0.5$ then the distance covered by the block before it stops is (Acceleration due to gravity $=10\text{ m s}^{-2}$ )

solution: Solution: Block stops on incline plane when its initial K.E is used in doing work against friction and partly it is converted into potential energy. As angle of incline is given $45^{\circ}$ so, distance covered on incline $(s)$ is related to height of block (h) as, $\Rightarrow \sin 45^{\circ}=\frac{h}{s}$ or $s=\sqrt{2} h$ Let block covers a distance $s$ over block and reaches up-to height $h$ . Then, $\text{Initial K.E of block} = \text{Work done against friction} + \text{Potential energy gained by block}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} m u^2 = \mu m g \cos \theta \cdot s + m g h$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} m u^2 = \mu m g \cos \theta \cdot \sqrt{2} \cdot h + m g h$ $\Rightarrow h = \frac{\; \frac{1}{2} m u^2}{\sqrt{2} \mu m g \cos \theta + m g}$ Here, initial $\text{K.E} = \frac{1}{2} m u^2 = 100\text{ J}$ $m=5\text{ kg},\ \theta=45^{\circ},\ g=10\text{ m/s}^2$ So, $h = \frac{100}{\sqrt{2} \times 0.5 \times 5 \times 10 \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + 5 \times 10}$ $= \frac{100}{50 \times 1.5} = \frac{4}{3}$ Hence, distance covered over block, $s=\sqrt{2} h$ $\Rightarrow s = \frac{\sqrt{2} \times 4}{3}\text{ m} = \frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{ m}$ © examsnet.com

question: A wheel is rotating freely at some angular speed. A second wheel initially at rest and with thrice the rotational inertia of the first, is suddenly coupled to the first wheel. The fraction of the original rotational kinetic energy lost is

solution: Solution: Let, $I_1=$ Inertia of first (rotating)  wheel $\omega_1=$ Angular speed of first wheel $I_2=3 I_1=$ Inertia of second wheel $\omega_2=0=$ Angular speed of second wheel let $\omega=$ Angular speed of coupled wheels. According to conservation of angular momentum, total initial angular momentum $=$ total final angular momentum $\Rightarrow I_1 \omega_1 + I_2 \times 0 = (I_1+I_2) \omega$ $\Rightarrow \omega = \frac{I_1 \omega_1}{I_1+I_2} = \frac{I_1 \omega_1}{I_1+3 I_1} \Rightarrow \omega = \frac{\omega_1}{4}$ Now, initial rotational energy of system is $K_1 = \frac{1}{2} I_1 \omega_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} I_2 (0)^2$ $\Rightarrow K_1 = \frac{1}{2} I_1 \omega_1^2$ Final rotational kinetic energy of system is $K_2 = \frac{1}{2} (I_1+I_2) \omega^2$ $= \frac{1}{2} (I_1+3 I_1) \cdot \frac{\omega_1^2}{16}$ or $K_2 = \frac{1}{4} K_1$ $= \frac{1}{2} \times 4 I_1 \times \frac{\omega_1^2}{16}$ $= \frac{1}{4} \left( \frac{1}{2} I_1 \omega_1^2 \right)$ Hence, fraction of lost energy $= \frac{\Delta K}{K_1} = \frac{K_1 - K_2}{K_1} = \frac{\frac{3}{4} K_1}{K_1}$ $= \frac{3}{4} = 0.75$ © examsnet.com

subject: Physics
question: Two wooden blocks of mass $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ rest on a frictionless table. A bullet of mass $m$ is fired at $M_{1}$ with speed $v$ which embedded in it and the two together finally collide with $M_{2}$ . Find the velocity of $M_{2}$ after collision. [Ignore any energy loss and treat the problem to be one dimensional]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: For an elastic collision of 2 masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ with initial velocities $u_1$ and $u_2$ , final velocities of masses after collision are $v_1 = \left(\frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right) u_1 + \frac{2 m_2 u_2}{(m_1+m_2)}$ and $v_2 = \left(\frac{m_2 - m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\right) u_2 + \frac{2 m_1 u_2}{m_1 + m_2}$ These are obtained as standard results by applying conservation of energy and momentum equations. Now, in given case at first bullet is embedded in mass $M_1$ . Let speed of bullet + Block system be $v_1$ after collision. Then by conservation of momentum we have. $m v = (m + M_1) v_1$ or $v_1 = \frac{m v}{m + M_1}$ Note Here we are not using standard result as first collision is perfectly inelastic. Now, bullet $+M_1$ strikes $M_2$ and it is given in problem that this collision is elastic. Now, by formula we have, $v_2 = \left(\frac{(m + M_1) - M_2}{m + M_1 + M_2}\right) v_1 + 0$ and $v_3 = \left(\frac{M_2 - (m + M_1)}{M_2 + m + M_1} \times 0\right) + \left(\frac{2 (m + M_1) v_1}{m + M_1 + M_2}\right)$ $\Rightarrow v_3 = \frac{2 (m + M_1)}{m + M_1 + M_2} \cdot \frac{m v}{(m + M_1)}$ $= \frac{2 m v}{m + M_1 + M_2}$ Note You can remember these standard and useful results for finding final velocities in case of elastic collisions. © examsnet.com

solution: Solution: Given, displacement of block, $x=5 t^{2}$ As, velocity $v=\frac{d x}{d t}$ Velocity of block, $v=\frac{d}{dt}(5 t^{2})$ $=5 \times 2 t=10 t\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ Now, velocity of block at $t=5\,\text{s}$ , $v_{2}=10 \times 5=50\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ and velocity of block at $t=3\,\text{s}$ is $v_{1}=10 \times 3=30\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ Also, velocity of block at $t=0\,\text{s}$ , $v_{0}=10 \times 0=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ Now, by work- K.E theorem, work done by a force = Change in kinetic energy So work done by force in first $3\,\text{sec}$ , $W_{1}=\frac{1}{2}m v_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m v_{0}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}m(v_{1}^{2}-v_{0}^{2})$ And work done by force in first $5\,\text{sec}$ , $W_{2}=\frac{1}{2}m v_{2}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m v_{0}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}m(v_{2}^{2}-v_{0}^{2})$ Hence, ratio $\frac{W_{1}}{W_{2}}=\frac{\frac{1}{2}m(v_{1}^{2}-v_{0}^{2})}{\frac{1}{2}m(v_{2}^{2}-v_{0}^{2})}$ $=\frac{v_{1}^{2}-v_{0}^{2}}{v_{2}^{2}-v_{0}^{2}}$ or $\frac{W_{1}}{W_{2}}=\frac{v_{1}^{2}}{v_{2}^{2}}$ $...[\text{As}, v_{0}=0]$ $\Rightarrow \frac{W_{1}}{W_{2}}=\left(\frac{30}{50}\right)^{2}=\frac{9}{25}$ © examsnet.com

question: A uniform rod of length $60\,\text{cm}$ is placed with one end in contact with the horizontal table and is then inclined at an angle $30^{\circ}$ to the horizontal and allowed to fall. The angular velocity of the rod when it becomes horizontal is (acceleration due to gravity $=10\,\text{ms}^{-2}$ )

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: As rod falls, its loss of gravitational potential energy appears as gain of angular rotational energy. If rod is rotating at angular speed $\omega$ when it is horizontal then, Rotational $K E = \text{Loss of gravitational PE}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2 = m g h$ $\ldots(i)$ Now for rod, Moment of inertia of a solid rod about its one end, $I = \frac{M L^2}{3}$ and $h = \frac{l}{2} \sin \theta$ $\ldots[\text{see fig } \theta = 30^{\circ}]$ $= \frac{l}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{l}{4}$ So from $\text{Eq. (i)}$ , we have $\frac{1}{2} M \frac{l^2}{3} \times \omega^2 = M g \frac{l}{4}$ $\Rightarrow \omega^2 = \frac{3}{2} \times \frac{g}{l}$ Here, $g = 10\,\text{m/s}^2$ and $l = 0.6\,\text{m}$ So, $\omega^2 = \frac{3}{2} \times \frac{10}{0.6} = 25$ or $\omega = 5\,\text{rad/s}$ © examsnet.com

question: A wheel undergoes a constant acceleration starting form rest at $t=0$ . The angular velocity of the wheel is $3.14\;\frac{\text{rad}}{\text{sec}}$ when $t=2\text{ s}$ . The accelerator is abruptly ceased at $t=20\text{ s}$ . The number of revolutions, wheel makes in the interval $t=0$ to $t=40\text{ s}$ is

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given, $\omega=314\;\frac{\text{rad}}{\text{s}}$ at $t=2\text{ s}$ Let $\alpha=$ constant angular acceleration Then using $\omega_1=\omega_0+\alpha t$ We have, $\omega_1=\alpha t$ $\cdots [\because \omega_0=0]$ $\therefore 314=\alpha(2)$ $\Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{314}{2}\;\frac{\text{rad}}{\text{s}^2}$ Now, angle covered in 20 seconds is given by, $\theta_1=\omega_0 t+\frac{1}{2}\alpha t^2$ $\Rightarrow\theta_1=\frac{1}{2}\alpha t^2$ So, $\theta_1=\frac{1}{2}\times\frac{314}{2}\times(20)^2=3.14\text{ rad}$ At $t=20\text{ s},\text{ angular speed of wheel,}$ $\Rightarrow\omega_2=\omega_0+\alpha t$ $\Rightarrow\omega_2=0+\frac{314}{2}\times 20$ As, acceleration does not operates after $t=20\text{ s}$ . So, wheel now rotates freely (with constant angular speed) upto $40\text{ s}$ . Angular displacement in radians covered in another 20s of freewheeling is $\theta_2\;=\omega_1\times t$ $=314\times 20=628\text{ rad}$ Total angle covered by wheel, $\theta=(314+628)\text{ rad}$ $=942\text{ rad}$ $\therefore$ Number of revolutions of wheel $n=\frac{\theta}{2\pi}=\frac{942}{2\pi}$ $=\frac{314\times 3}{2\times 314}=150$ © examsnet.com

question: A block of mass $100 \mathrm{g}$ is connected to an elastic spring of spring constant $450 \mathrm{Nm}^{-1}$ oscillates vertically. question: As shown in the figure, two spherical cavities are made in the uniform solid sphere of radius $R$ . The boundaries of the cavities touch at the centre of the sphere. The centers of the cavities and the sphere lie on the $x$ -axis. The mass of the solid sphere before the cavities were created was $M$ . solution: Solution: Radius of sphere given $=R$ Mass of sphere $=M$ Density of sphere, $d=\frac{M}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3}$ Radius of each of cavity $=\frac{R}{2}$ Mass of each of portion removed to create a cavity $=$ density $\times$ volume $=\frac{M}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3} \times \frac{4}{3}\pi \left(\frac{R}{2}\right)^3 = \frac{M}{8}$ Now, force of gravity on $m$ , $F=$ force due to complete sphere of mass $M$ -force of mass of cavity of sphere Centre at $A$ - force of mass of cavity of sphere Centre at $B$ . $=\frac{G M m}{d^2}=\frac{G M' m}{\left(d+\frac{R}{2}\right)^2}-\frac{G M' m}{\left(d-\frac{R}{2}\right)^2}$ $\Rightarrow F=\frac{G M m}{d^2}-\frac{GM m}{8\left(d+\frac{R}{2}\right)^2}-\frac{G M m}{8\left(d-\frac{R}{2}\right)^2}$ $=G M m \left(\frac{1}{d^2}-\frac{1}{8\left(d+\frac{R}{2}\right)^2}-\frac{1}{8\left(d-\frac{R}{2}\right)^2}\right)$ $=\frac{G M m}{d^2}\left(1-\frac{1}{8\left(1+\frac{R}{2d}\right)^2}-\frac{1}{8\left(1-\frac{R}{2d}\right)^2}\right)$ © examsnet.com

question: A circular film of a liquid has an area of $10\,\mathrm{cm}^2$ . If the work done in making its radius two times the initial radius is $8 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{J}$ , the surface tension of the liquid is $\left(1+\;\frac{1}{a}\right)\,\mathrm{Nm}^{-1}$ . The value of $\alpha$ is

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: If radius $(r)$ of a circle made two times $(2 r)$ then change in area $=\pi(2 r)^2-\pi r^2$ $=3\pi r^2=3\times\;\text{ initial area }\;$ Here, initial area of soap film, $A_1=10\,\mathrm{cm}^2$ Final area has a radius twice that of initial radius. So, change in area $\triangle A=3A_1=3\times10\,\mathrm{cm}^2$ $=3\times10\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}^2$ $=3\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}^2$ As, a liquid film has two surfaces (one top and other bottom). Change in surface energy or work done, $W=2\triangle A\times T$ $T=$ Surface tension or $T=\frac{W}{2\triangle A}$ Here, $W=8\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{J}$ $\Delta A=30\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}^2$ So, surface tension of Liquid, $T=\frac{8\times10^{-3}}{2\times3\times10^{-3}}$ $=\frac{8}{6}=\;\frac{4}{3}=1+\frac{1}{3}\,\mathrm{Nm}^{-1}$ Hence, $\alpha=3$ © examsnet.com

question: A monatomic gas $\left(r=\;\frac{5}{3}\right)$ at a pressure of $4\,\text{atm}$ is compressed adiabatically so that its temperature rises from $27^{\circ}\,\text{C}$ to $327^{\circ}\,\text{C}$ . The pressure of the gas in its final state is

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: For an adiabatic change, $p V^\gamma =\;\text{ constant }\;$ $\Rightarrow T^\gamma p^{1-\gamma} =\;\text{ constant or }\; T_1^\gamma, p_1^{1-\gamma}=T_2^\gamma \cdot p_2^{1-\gamma}$ $\Rightarrow p_2^{1-\gamma}= \left(\frac{T_1}{T_2}\right)^\gamma \cdot p_1^{1-\gamma}$ $\Rightarrow p_2= \left(\frac{T_1}{T_2}\right)^{\frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}} \cdot p_1$ $\;\text{ Here, }\; p_1=4\,\text{atm} ; \gamma=\frac{5}{3}$ $T_1=27^{\circ}\,\text{C}=300\,\text{K}$ $T_2=327^{\circ}\,\text{C}=600\,\text{K}$ Now, substituting values in Eq. (i), we get $p_2= \left(\frac{300}{600}\right)^{\frac{\frac{5}{3}}{1-\frac{5}{3}}} \times 4 = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{-5}{2}} \times 2^2$ $=2^{2+\frac{5}{2}} =2^{\frac{9}{2}}$ Hence, the pressure of the gas in its final state is $2^{\frac{9}{2}}$ atm. © examsnet.com

solution: Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let $I = \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^{2} - x^{5}}}$ $I = \int \frac{1}{x \sqrt{1 - x^{3}}} dx$ Let $x^{3} = \sin^{2} t$ $3 x^{2} dx = 2 \sin t \cos t dt$ $\Rightarrow I = \frac{1}{3} \int \frac{3 x^{2} dx}{x^{3} \sqrt{1 - x^{3}}}$ $= \frac{2}{3} \int \frac{1}{\sin^{2} t \cos t} \sin t \cos t dt$ $= \frac{2}{3} \int \csc t dt$ $= \frac{2}{3} \log |\csc t - \cot t| + C$ $= \frac{2}{3} \log \left| \frac{1 - \cos t}{\sin t} \right| + C$ $= \frac{2}{3} \log \left| \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - \sin^{2} t}}{\sqrt{\sin^{2} t}} \right| + C$ $= \frac{1}{3} \log \left( \left| \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - x^{3}}}{\sqrt{x^{3}}} \right|^{2} \right) + C$ Here, $f(x) = \left| \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - x^{3}}}{\sqrt{x^{3}}} \right|^{2}$ $f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \left| \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{3}}}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{3/2}} \right|^{2}$ $= \left( \frac{1 - \frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{8}}}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}} \right)^{2} = (\sqrt{8} - \sqrt{7})^{2}$ From option (a) $\colon \left( \frac{\sqrt{8} - \sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{8} + \sqrt{7}} \right) \times \left( \frac{\sqrt{8} - \sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{8} - \sqrt{7}} \right)$ $= (\sqrt{8} - \sqrt{7})^{2}$ © examsnet.com

solution: Solution: 👈: Video Solution Let $I = \int (1+x) \log (1+x^{2}) \, dx$ Using by parts $\log (1+x^{2}) \left[ \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x \right] - \int \frac{2x}{1+x^{2}} \times \left( \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x \right) \, dx$ $= \left( \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x \right) \log (1+x^{2}) - \int \frac{x^{2} (x+2)}{1+x^{2}} \, dx$ $= \left( \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x \right) \log (1+x^{2}) - \int \frac{x^{3} + 2x^{2}}{1+x^{2}} \, dx$ $= \left( \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x \right) \log (1+x^{2}) - \int (x+2) - \frac{x+2}{1+x^{2}} \, dx$ $= \left( \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x \right) \log (1+x^{2}) - \left( \frac{x^{2}}{2} + 2x \right) + \frac{1}{2} \int \frac{2x}{1+x^{2}} \, dx$ $+ 2 \int \frac{1}{1+x^{2}} \, dx$ $= \left( \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x \right) \log (1+x^{2}) - \frac{x^{2}}{2} - 2x +$ $\frac{1}{2} \log (1+x^{2})$ $+ 2 \tan^{-1} x$ $= \left( \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x + \frac{1}{2} \right) \log (1+x^{2}) - \frac{x^{2}}{2} - 2x + 2 \tan^{-1} x + C$ $\text{Compare I with } \left( x + \frac{x^{2}}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \right)$ $\log (1+x^{2}) + g(x) + C, \text{ we get }$ $g(x) = -2x - \frac{x^{2}}{2} + 2 \tan^{-1} x$ © examsnet.com

solution: Solution: The given situation is shown as; For a system of charges potential energy is given by $U=\sum\limits_{i=j} \frac{K q_i q_j}{r_{ij}}$ ⇒ Hence for given system potential energy, $U=\frac{K q_1 q_2}{r_{12}} + \frac{K q_2 q_2}{r_{13}}$ $=\frac{K(-q)(q)}{x} + \frac{K(q)(Q)}{x} + \frac{K(-q)(Q)}{\sqrt{2}x}$ $=\frac{Kq}{x} \left(-q+Q-\frac{Q}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$ So, potential energy will be zero if $-q+Q-\frac{Q}{\sqrt{2}}=0$ or $Q\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)=q$ ⇒ $Q=(\sqrt{2}-1)=\sqrt{2}q$ ⇒ $Q=\frac{\sqrt{2}q}{\sqrt{2}-1}$ © examsnet.com

subject: Physics
question: A bar magnet of length $16\ \text{cm}$ is placed in the magnetic meridian with the $\text{N}$ - pole pointing towards geographical north. Two neutral points separated by $12\ \text{cm}$ are obtained on the equatorial line of the magnet. If the horizontal component of earth's magnetic field $=3.2 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{T}$ , then the pole strength of magnet is

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: The given situation is shown below. Note Earth's field goes from South to North: At neutral point horizontal component of earth, is opposed by field of magnet so, at neutral point, $B_H=B_{\text{magnet}}$ ⇒ $B_H = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \cdot \frac{M}{r^3}$ Where, $M=$ magnetic dipole moment of magnet and $r=$ distance of neutral point from centre of magnet Here, $B_H = 3.2\times 10^{-5}\text{T}$ $r-6\ \text{cm}=6\times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}$ Hence, $3.2 \times 10^{-5} = 10^{-7} \times \frac{M}{(6 \times 10^{-2})^3}$ ⇒ $M=\frac{3.2 \times 10^{-5} \times 216 \times 10^{-6}}{10^{-7}}$ $=6. \times 10^{-2}\ \text{A-m}^2$ If length of magnet is taken $2l$ , then $M=m \cdot 2l$ , (∵ m= pole strength) Here, $2l=16\ \text{cm}=16\times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}$ ⇒ $6.9 \times 10^{-2} = m \times 16 \times 10^{-2}$ ⇒ $m = \frac{6.9}{16} = 0.43\ \text{A-m} \simeq 0.5\ \text{A-m}$ © examsnet.com

question: The power consumed when $10\ \mathrm{V}$ voltage is applied to a series combination of 10 resistors of each $1\ \Omega$ is $P_s$ and the power consumed when the same $10\ \mathrm{V}$ is applied to the parallel combination of these 10 resistors is $P_p$ . The value of $\;\frac{P_s}{P_p}$ is

solution: Solution: The given circuit can be shown as. Total resistance in above case, $R_S=R_1+R_2+.......+R_{10}$ ⇒ $R_s = 10\Omega$ Current in circuit , $I=\frac{V}{R_s}$ ⇒ $I=\frac{10}{10} = 1\ \mathrm{A}$ Power consumption of circuit, $P_s=I^2\times 10\times 10\Omega$ In second case, $\frac{1}{R_P} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + .....$ ⇒ $\frac{1}{R_P} = \frac{10}{1}$ ⇒ $R_P - \frac{1}{10}\Omega$ Power consumption, $P_P = \frac{V^2}{R_P} = \frac{100}{\frac{1}{10}} = 10^3\ \mathrm{W}$ ⇒ $\frac{P_S}{P_P} = \frac{10}{1000} = 0.01$ © examsnet.com

question: Two long wires carrying current is $8 A$ and $6 A$ along $x$ axes and $y$ axes respectively. The magnetic field at the point $(2\hat{i}+4\hat{j})$ is (Take $\mu_{0}=4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ SI unit)

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: The situation given can be shown as Magnetic field at some point $P$ with position vector $r$ due to a straight long current carrying wire is given by $B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}$ Where, $d=$ Perpendicular distance of point from wire. Here, $r=2\hat{i}+4\hat{j}\,\text{m}$ ⇒ for wire on X - axis, $d=d_x=4\,\text{m}$ and for wire on Y-axis $d=d_y=2\,\text{m}$ As magnetic fields due to wires along $X$ and along $Y$ -axis are in opposite direction ( $RH$ rule) so, $B_{\text{net}} = B+B_x$ $=\frac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi d_y}(\hat{k}) + \frac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi d_x}(-\hat{k})$ $= \frac{\mu_0}{2\pi} \left(\frac{I_2}{d_y} - \frac{I_1}{d_x}\right) \hat{k}$ $= \frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7}}{2\pi} \left(\frac{6}{2} - \frac{8}{4}\right) \hat{k}$ $= 2 \times 10^{-7} \hat{k} \,\text{T}$ ∴ $\left|B_{\text{net}}\right| = 2 \times 10^{-7} \,\text{T}$ © examsnet.com

(ii) we get, $\frac{1}{2} m (3v_1)^2 = \frac{hc}{200\times 10^{-9}} - \phi_0$ or $9\left(\frac{1}{2} mv^2_1\right) = \frac{hc}{200\times 10^{-9}} - \phi_0$ Substituting for $\frac{1}{2} mv^2_1$ from eq.(i) in above we get, $9\left(\frac{hc}{600\times 10^{-9}}\right) - \phi_0 = \frac{hc}{200\times 10^{-9}} - \phi_0$ ⇒ $\frac{hc}{10^{-7}} \left(\frac{9}{6} - \frac{1}{2}\right) = 8\phi_0$ $\text{Work function, } \phi_0 = \frac{hc}{8} \times 10^7 \text{ J}$ © examsnet.com

solution: Solution: In a C.E transisator voltage gain, $A_y$ = Current gain $(\alpha_{AC})\times$ Resistance gaing $\left(\frac{R_1}{R_{BE}}\right)$ ⇒ $A_V = \alpha_{AC} \times \frac{R_C}{R_B} \Rightarrow \frac{V_{\text{output}}}{V_{\text{input}}} = \alpha_{AC} \times \frac{R_C}{R_B}$ Substituting given values, we get ⇒ $\frac{2.5}{0.02} = \alpha_{AC} = \frac{2.5 \times 1.5}{0.02 \times 25} = 75$ So, current gaing (or current amplification) $=75$ © examsnet.com
